meaning_missing.guide: A word in scope with no meaning senses (or, for Greek, no Mounce entry). Pull it through the spine route and name the row, or give the reason it is not needed for this reading.

not_read.guide: A verse with no observation and no strand face. Read it in its passage; record what it states about the inner being (a new observation), name an existing observation that already covers it, or give the reason it holds nothing.

file_lines: _analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-v3-20261007.md:293   - leaders: "Moses chose able men out of all Israel and made them heads" (Exo 18:25)

new.text: People select men for battle, leadership or a task, and the word marks fitness: "Moses chose able men out of all Israel and made them heads over the people" (Exo 18:25); "700 chosen men who were left-handed; every one could sling a stone at a hair and not miss" (Judg 20:16); "300,000 choice men, fit for war, able to handle spear and shield" (2Ch 25:5). The same word names the men "chosen from the assembly, well-known men" who rose up against Moses (Num 16:2).
new.meaning: Here choosing is a judgement of ability: a leader weighs others and takes the fit for a task; being chosen does not secure faithfulness.
new.setting: Exodus to Chronicles, mostly armies and musters (Jos 8:3, Joshua's 30,000 for Ai).
new.implication: Choosing can rest on assessed capacity.
new.parties: leaders (Moses, Joshua, Saul, David, kings); the men chosen

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-2c-reading-batch2-others-ot-v1-20261008.md:25 The verse closes a long dispute over who God has chosen. It begins in Numbers 16. Korah and 250 chiefs, *"chosen from the assembly, well-known men"* (16:2; *qārîʾ*, H7148, "called"), rise up: *"Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the Lord?"* (16:3). Moses answers with God's choosing: *"The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him"* (16:5), and *"the man whom the Lord chooses shall be the holy one"* (16:7).

new.text: God chooses a person for a task or office: priests and Levites, the king, David, Solomon, the servant, witnesses. Choosing goes with bringing near: "The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him" (Num 16:5); "Blessed is the one you choose and bring near" (Psa 65:4). The choice is shown, not argued: "the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout" (Num 17:5). It is followed by a charge: "the Lord has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it" (1Ch 28:10). In the servant it is joined to God's soul and Spirit: "my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him" (Isa 42:1; Mat 12:18).
new.meaning: God's choosing of a person brings that person near and lays a task on them; the chosen still has to act.
new.setting: Numbers (Korah), Samuel and Chronicles (the kings passed over and chosen, 1Sa 16:8-10), the Psalms, Isaiah, Haggai; Act 10:41, witnesses chosen beforehand.
new.implication: A choosing will issues in nearness and charge, and can name the chosen as a son (1Ch 28:6).
new.parties: God; priests, Levites, kings, the servant, witnesses

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-others-around-choosing-account-v1-20261008.md:12 **Scope:** The account covers people who stand near a choice someone else made: at what was chosen, turned toward it, set against it, standing with the chosen, or knowing of the choice. In all but one of the readings the chooser is God. In 1Sa 20:30 it is Jonathan. God's own acts in reply (Num 17:5; Isa 45:4–5; 49:7; Jer 33:25–26; Rom 11:8; 1Pe 2:8) belong to 13.1 under rule 72. They are named here only where they answer what the others did. Readings beyond what a verse says are marked "I read".

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-others-around-choosing-account-v1-20261008.md:60 **Grumbling, and seeking more.** When God's choice of Aaron was challenged, Moses named what lay under it: *"would you seek the priesthood also?"* (Num 16:10). The grumbling at Aaron was against God: *"What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"* (16:11), and God calls it *"the grumblings … which they grumble against you"*, to be made to *"cease from me"* (17:5). Psalm 106 names the inner act: *"men in the camp were jealous of Moses and Aaron"* (Psa 106:16). God's reply was to make the choice plain, with the staff that sprouted. Then the grumbling became terror: *"Are we all to perish?"* (Num 17:13).

new.text: God chooses a place "to make his name dwell there" (Deu 12:11), and the choosing carries his own presence: "My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (2Ch 7:16). The people's offerings, eating, rejoicing, judgement, reading of the law and prayer are all directed to the place he chooses. The choice can be cast off, "I will cast off this city that I have chosen" (2Ki 23:27), and made again: "the Lord will again comfort Zion and again choose Jerusalem" (Zec 1:17).
new.meaning: God's choosing fixes where he sets his name and his heart; the people's acts, and their repentance with all their heart and soul (1Ki 8:48; 2Ch 6:38), turn toward what he has chosen.
new.setting: Deuteronomy's law of the one place; Kings and Chronicles narrow it to Jerusalem and the house; Zechariah after the exile (Zec 3:2: the choice named against the accuser).
new.implication: A choice can be bound to presence and attention, and can be withdrawn and renewed.

Batch 1 read Deuteronomy 12 in full. The forms of words differ: 12:5 has *"out of all your tribes"*, 12:14 *"in one of your tribes"*, and 23:16 *"within one of your towns"*. In 23:16 the chooser is the escaped slave. The reading does not settle whether the shared phrase is more than a form of words. It stays held.

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch3-own-accord-together-v1-20261007.md:28 The phrase is a weighty one in Deuteronomy. *"the place that he shall choose within one of your towns"* has the same shape as the phrase Deuteronomy uses for the Lord’s own choosing: *"the place that the Lord your God will choose out of all your tribes"* (12:5); *"the place that the Lord will choose in one of your tribes"* (12:14). The words (place, that, choose, in one of your …) are the same (H4725, H0977). I read this as the law giving the escaped slave, in his own small measure, the kind of choosing the Lord keeps for his own dwelling. The verse does not draw the comparison.

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-others-around-choosing-account-v1-20261008.md:34 **Carefulness, against presumption.** When a case is *"too difficult for you"* (17:8), the decision is sought at the place. What is asked of the person then is *"you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you"* (17:10), and not to turn *"to the right hand or to the left"* (17:11). Presumption is the opposite, and the man who acts presumptuously dies. The end is that *"all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again"* (17:13). I read this as a person's own judgement reaching its limit and being asked to yield. The passage gives the limit (*"too difficult for you"*) and the carefulness. It does not describe the inner struggle.

new.text: A person chooses the Lord, his ways and the good: "choose this day whom you will serve" (Jos 24:15), and the choice is witnessed: "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the Lord" (Jos 24:22); "I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me" (Psa 119:30); "who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant" (Isa 56:4). Choosing needs knowing and instruction: "when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good" (Isa 7:15); "Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose" (Psa 25:12). It can be done together: "Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good" (Job 34:4). Preference is stated: "I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God" (Psa 84:10); "choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin" (Heb 11:25).
new.meaning: The person's choosing of the good rests on knowing and is taught; it binds the chooser as a witness and is kept by holding fast.
new.setting: Joshua at Shechem, the Psalms, Isaiah, Job, Hebrews 11 (Moses).
new.implication: Knowing comes before good choosing, and a choice made can be held against the chooser.
new.parties: the people; the psalmist; the eunuchs; Moses

The celebrating had stopped at Uzzah's death, when David was angry, afraid and unwilling (6:8–10). It came back when he heard of the Lord's blessing (6:12).

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-being-chosen-account-v1-20261008.md:66 The chosen live before God's sight, not others'. David answers Michal, who measured him by *"the eyes of his servants' female servants"* (2Sa 6:20): *"It was before the Lord, who chose me"*, and *"I will be abased in your eyes"* (6:21–22). The purpose of the choosing in Ephesians is to be holy and blameless *"before him"* (Eph 1:4).

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-others-around-choosing-account-v1-20261008.md:64 **Contempt in the heart.** Michal *"saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart"* (2Sa 6:16). The contempt is inward before it is spoken. When it comes out, its measure is honour before others: *"before the eyes of his servants' female servants"* (6:20). David answers by naming the choosing: *"It was before the Lord, who chose me above your father"* (6:21).

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch2-psalm-promise-v1-20261007.md:108 **For the next batches:** batch 3 is people choosing of their own accord, and choosing together (Deu 23:16, 2Sa 19:38, 2Cor 8:17, Act 6:5, Act 15:22 and 25), with the wisdom sayings Pro 3:31 and 16:16. These are mostly not choices between God and other gods. Whether they show the same tie to what the eyes see, to delight and to knowing is to be read from them.
_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch3-own-accord-together-v1-20261007.md:7 **Verses:** Deu 23:16 · 2Sa 19:38 · 2Cor 8:17 · Act 6:5 · Act 15:22, 25 · Pro 3:31 · Pro 16:16.
_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch3-own-accord-together-v1-20261007.md:37 ## 2 Samuel 19:38 — "whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me"

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch3-own-accord-together-v1-20261007.md:170 - **Choosing as a person's own freedom, honoured.** In Deu 23:16 and 2Sa 19:38 the ground is the chooser's own good: *"wherever it suits him"*, *"whatever seems good to you"*. Others are bound to honour it. This is a face not seen in batches 1–2, where the choosing was between the Lord and something else. Here "good in your eyes" is honoured. In Jos 24:15, "evil in your eyes" was where the choice against the Lord could start. The same expression changes character with the setting (#1919).
_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-v3-20261007.md:279   - "all that you desire of me I will do for you" (2Sa 19:38)

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choosing-account-v1-20261007.md:11 - [batch 3](m64-choose-reading-batch3-own-accord-together-v1-20261007.md): Deu 23:16, 2Sa 19:38, 2Cor 8:17, Act 6:5, Act 15:22 and 25, Pro 3:31, Pro 16:16
_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choosing-account-v1-20261007.md:26   - *"desire"*: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2Sa 19:38)

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choosing-account-v1-20261007.md:56 **What is good to the chooser.** Two verses make the chooser's own good the ground, and honour it: *"wherever it suits him"* (Deu 23:16) and *"whatever seems good to you"* (2Sa 19:38). In Hebrew both say "the good" to him, or in his eyes.

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choosing-account-v1-20261007.md:77 Yet "good in your eyes" is not always the wrong measure. When the king says *"whatever seems good to you"* to the old man who served him (2Sa 19:38), the chooser's own eyes are honoured. The setting changes what the same expression means. (See "What changes the character" below.)

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choosing-account-v1-20261007.md:105 Choosing is a freedom a person can lose, and Scripture gives it back. The escaped slave *"shall dwell with you … in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him"* (Deu 23:16). The king hands the choice to the man who fed him in the wilderness: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2Sa 19:38).
_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choosing-account-v1-20261007.md:172   - It is the chooser's own good, honoured by the king (2Sa 19:38).

The psalm's "desires life … that he may see good" and Job's "never again see good" are one phrase. **I read** that the want for life is a want to see good. _analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch2-psalm-promise-v1-20261007.md:35 Then comes the verse: *"Who is the man who fears the Lord? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"* (v12). The word "instruct" is the same in v8 and v12 (H3384B). The person who chooses here does not make up the way. The way to choose is taught, and the one who is taught it is the one who fears the Lord. The fear comes first, then the teaching, then the choice. The verse does not say the man chooses well on his own; it says the Lord instructs him in what he should choose.

Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"* (Psa 25:12). The teaching comes from who the Lord is: *"Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he instructs sinners in the way"* (25:8). _analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choosing-account-v1-20261007.md:20 Scripture does not stop to define choosing. In these verses it shows choosing as an act with two sides. The clearest sentence is about a child: *"when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (Isa 7:15). Refusing and choosing are one act, seen from either side. The man the book of Job calls blameless is described by his refusing: he *"feared God and turned away from evil"* (Job 1:1). The father in Proverbs puts the choice entirely in the negative: *"do not choose any of his ways"* (Pro 3:31).

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch1-isaiah-v1-20261007.md:25 The sign is given anyway, and at its centre is a child who has what Ahaz lacked: *"He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (v15). The act is one act with two sides:

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch1-isaiah-v1-20261007.md:130 - **Refusing is choosing (Isa 7:15–16).** The act is one act with two sides, and refusing can go either way. The child refuses the evil. Ahaz refuses the sign, and the people refuse the gentle waters (8:6), with the same verb. This sharpens the test reading of Isa 65:12, which said that not answering and not listening are already choosing: in Isa 8:6 the refusal is named outright.

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch1-isaiah-v1-20261007.md:131 - **Choosing rests on knowing how (Isa 7:15).** It is a knowing *how* to tell evil from good and turn. In Isa 1 the oracle opens with its absence: *"Israel does not know, my people do not understand"* (1:3).

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch1-isaiah-v1-20261007.md:133 - **The choice is laid out as an offer, with both outcomes (Isa 1:16–20).** *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"*; *"willing"* or *"refuse"*; eat, or be eaten. In Isa 7:15 the right choice also ends in eating.

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch2-psalm-promise-v1-20261007.md:38 - *"His soul shall abide in well-being, and his offspring shall inherit the land"* (v13). "Well-being" here (H2896B) is the same word as *"the good"* in Isaiah 7:15, *"refuse the evil and choose the good"*. The man taught the way he should choose has his soul *"abide"*, lodge or stay, in the good.

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch2-psalm-promise-v1-20261007.md:41 The psalmist then turns his eyes: *"My eyes are ever toward the Lord, for he will pluck my feet out of the net"* (v15). Where the eyes are turned decides where the feet are kept from.

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch2-psalm-promise-v1-20261007.md:97 - **The good chosen is the good the soul lives in.** Isaiah 7:15 has *"choose the good"*, and Psalm 25:13 has *"His soul shall abide in well-being"*. It is the same word (H2896B). I read this as the good that is chosen becoming the place where the soul lives. Each verse says its own half; neither refers to the other.

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch3-own-accord-together-v1-20261007.md:41 Barzillai declines, and his reason is about his own inner capacity: *"I am this day eighty years old. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women?"* (v35). The Hebrew is "know between good and evil" (H3045 with H0996, H2896B, H7451A). It is the same pairing as Isaiah 7:15–16, *"knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"*. Here it is the knowing of taste and pleasure, and Barzillai says that at eighty it has gone. The same words, put to the palate rather than to right and wrong, mark a change of face (#1919).

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch3-own-accord-together-v1-20261007.md:175 - **The knowing of good and evil has more than one face.** In Isa 7:15 it is the knowing that grounds choosing the good. In 2Sa 19:35 the same words are the palate's knowing of pleasant and unpleasant, and they fade with age.

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch4-job-weighed-by-another-v1-20261007.md:79 - **The refusing word comes back.** *"because you reject it"* uses H3988A, the same verb as *"refuse the evil"* in Isaiah 7:15. Elihu says Job is refusing, and that God will not repay on Job's terms because of it.

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch4-job-weighed-by-another-v1-20261007.md:129 - **The refusing verb returns at the end.** Elihu's *"you reject"* and Job's *"I despise … and repent"* are the same verb (34:33; 42:6), the verb of *"refuse the evil"* (Isa 7:15). In Job the choice is made when *"now my eye sees you"* (42:5). This stands beside the test reading of Jos 24, where the people chose from what they had seen.

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choosing-account-v1-20261007.md:20 Scripture does not stop to define choosing. In these verses it shows choosing as an act with two sides. The clearest sentence is about a child: *"when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (Isa 7:15). Refusing and choosing are one act, seen from either side. The man the book of Job calls blameless is described by his refusing: he *"feared God and turned away from evil"* (Job 1:1). The father in Proverbs puts the choice entirely in the negative: *"do not choose any of his ways"* (Pro 3:31).

The oracle around that verse shows refusing going both ways. Ahaz refuses the Lord's offer of a sign with pious words: *"I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test"* (Isa 7:12). The people *"refused the waters of Shiloah that flow gently"* (8:6). The right refusing and the wrong refusing are set in one oracle, each with its own consequence.

They are recorded here because each one answers what the others did.

The child refuses the evil. Ahaz refuses the sign, and the people refuse the gentle waters (8:6), with the same verb. This sharpens the test reading of Isa 65:12, which said that not answering and not listening are already choosing: in Isa 8:6 the refusal is named outright.

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch2-psalm-promise-v1-20261007.md:65 Then he describes the eunuchs he means: *"who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"* (v4). The word "please" is H2654A, the same word as *"delight"* in Isaiah 65:12 and 66:4 (*"chose what I did not delight in"*, *"chose that in which I did not delight"*). Here the choosing goes the other way. These choose what the Lord delights in. The measure is the same as in those two oracles, the Lord's delight, and here it is met.

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-test-reading-v1-20261007.md:94 The answer turns on their own word: *"I will destine you to the sword"* (v12). _analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch1-isaiah-v1-20261007.md:98 Against that stands worship that looks right and is not: *"He who slaughters an ox is like one who kills a man; he who sacrifices a lamb, like one who breaks a dog’s neck"* … *"like one who blesses an idol"* (v3). The outward act is the same as before; what has gone wrong is inside. The verse says where: *"These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations."* Choosing and the soul’s delight stand side by side. They chose their own ways, and their soul (H5315) takes pleasure in what the Lord calls abominations.

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch2-psalm-promise-v1-20261007.md:78 What follows in the chapter is the opposite. Israel's own watchmen *"are all without knowledge"*. new.text: A person chooses against God: other gods, "the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you" (Judg 10:14); their own ways, "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isa 66:3); what God does not delight in (Isa 65:12). The verses name what drives or follows such choosing: "your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty" (Job 15:5); "Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways" (Pro 3:31); "this you have chosen rather than affliction" (Job 36:21). Shame follows: "you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen" (Isa 1:29); "an abomination is he who chooses you" (Isa 41:24).
new.meaning: Wrong choosing is taught by iniquity, drawn by envy, joined to the soul's delight and made to escape affliction; it ends in shame and makes the chooser like what is chosen.
new.setting: Judges (new gods, Judg 5:8), Job, Proverbs, Isaiah.
new.implication: The will is shaped by what teaches it, what it envies and what the soul delights in.

items.text: For they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord,
file_lines: _analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch3-own-accord-together-v1-20261007.md:12 - 2Cor 8:1–24

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch3-own-accord-together-v1-20261007.md:60 The chapter is about giving to the poor saints. It opens with the Macedonians: *"in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity"* (v2). They gave *"according to their means … and beyond their means, of their own accord"* (v3). That is the same word as in v17 (G0830, *authairetos*, "self-chosen"). The order of their giving is set out: *"they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us"* (v5). Their own accord and the will of God stand side by side in one sentence.

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-batch3-own-accord-together-v1-20261007.md:171 - **Own accord alongside God's working.** Titus goes *"of his own accord"* after God *"put into the heart"* the care (2Cor 8:16–17). The Macedonians give *"of their own accord"*, having given themselves to the Lord *"by the will of God"* (8:3, 5). Both are named and neither cancels the other. This sits with batch 2 (the way to choose is taught) and the test (Psa 119:32, the heart enlarged by God).
_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choose-reading-v3-20261007.md:285   - "they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord" (2Cor 8:3)
_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choosing-account-v1-20261007.md:36 - **G0830, "of one's own accord".** One word, literally "self-chosen" (2Cor 8:3, 17).

_analytics/Clusters/M64 - will-resolve/m64-choosing-account-v1-20261007.md:92 The Macedonians gave *"of their own accord"*, and the order of their giving is set out: *"they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us"* (8:3, 5). The church's choice is joined to the Spirit's in the same verb: *"it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us"* (Act 15:28). The psalmist chooses, and asks God to give the room to carry it out: *"I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart!"* (Psa 119:32). I read these verses as saying that what God puts into the heart becomes the person's own. The verses name both and do not explain how they fit.
